title: food as practice
hook: pure food, a clear mind, a steady memory, every knot loosened: one chain in the Chandogya

segments.voice: Yesterday, food as practice and Uddalaka's ember: the mind, my dear, is made of food.

Pure food. A clear mind. A steady memory. Every knot loosened. That's a chain, link by link, and it sits at the close of the seventh chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad. The chapter opens with the sage Narada admitting that, for all his learning, he's still in sorrow. It ends with this chain, and with a teacher showing him the far shore beyond darkness. Yesterday a hungry student got his memory back after a meal. Today the same Upanishad takes that thought much further, on the last of our food days.
screen: `PURE FOOD, CLEAR MIND.` → `STEADY MEMORY, KNOTS LOOSENED.` → `THE FAR SHORE BEYOND DARKNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, paraphrased. When food is pure, the inner being is pure. When the inner being is pure, memory becomes steady. When memory is steady, all the knots are loosened. In Sanskrit it begins aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih. Ahara is what's taken in. Sattva is the inner being, the mind in its clearest sense. Notice three things. First, the direction. It runs from the plate inward: from something as plain as a meal toward something as large as freedom. Second, memory here isn't remembering where the keys are. Readers in the Vedanta tradition take it as a steady remembering of what matters, of who one really is. Third, the knots. The text doesn't name them. Readers have heard in them the tangles that bind a person: craving, confusion, old fears. Every one loosened, the line says. Then the scholar's turn. Shankara, the Vedanta teacher, reads ahara more widely than food: everything gathered in, what the eyes take in, what the ears take in, what the mind is fed all day. Pure intake, not just a pure plate. So the chain reaches a screen as easily as a kitchen. Now the look back. Bhrigu's vow. Eating in measure. A meal with the mind on it. The three kinds of food and the hour after. The guest at the door. The ember. And this chain. And wider, over the lens so far: the doshas, held as a way of noticing; the daily routine; the seasons met with care; and food, from the plate all the way to the knots.
screen: `PURE FOOD, PURE INNER BEING` · `STEADY MEMORY, KNOTS LOOSENED` · `AHARA: ALL THAT'S TAKEN IN` · `FROM THE PLATE TO THE KNOTS`

segments.voice: Go back through the day so far, not only meals: what the eyes took in, a screen, a street, a face, and what the ears took in, voices, music, news, letting each pass without grading it. Then find one knot somewhere, a tightness something left behind, and with each breath out let it loosen a little, if it will. If you pray, hold that knot in prayer.
Food as practice. In the Chandogya's chain, pure intake, a clear inner being, steady memory, and every knot loosened. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. Ahara is everything taken in, not just the plate. Day one thousand three hundred thirteen, and the food days are done.

howItsDone: Some Hindus cite the Chandogya's line aharashuddhau sattvashuddhih to explain care about what and how they eat, and Vedanta teachers following Shankara apply it to everything a person takes in through the senses.
